outcome: No settlement has been accepted since 26 January 2024. The window holds one unrefereed claimed proof that no 3×3 magic square of distinct square integers exists (Oscar Hill, arXiv 2510.08286, first posted 9 Oct 2025, latest version 7 Apr 2026), which no journal, referee report or citing work I found has taken up; the 2026 Auel–Singer paper still calls the distinct-integer question open and does not cite Hill, and the Wikipedia article (edited 23 Sep 2026 per the page) still lists the problem as unsolved. Neighbouring in-window results (magic squares of squares of every order n ≥ 4, June 2024; K-multimagic bounds, June 2024; the algebraic geometry of the associated surface, Sept 2026) do not decide the 3×3 distinct case.
problem_asks: Read from the statement alone: (1) whether a 3×3 magic square exists, i.e. a 3×3 array whose three rows, three columns and two main diagonals all have the same sum; (2) whether all nine entries can be perfect square numbers (the statement does not say integers; the literature treats integer squares and separately rational, Gaussian-integer and finite-field variants; whether 0 counts as a perfect square is not stated); (3) whether the nine entries can be pairwise distinct; (4) the question asks whether such a square 'can be constructed', a yes/no existence question, so an affirmative answer is a construction and a negative answer is a proof of impossibility. The problem asks for all of (1) to (4) together: one 3×3 array of nine pairwise distinct perfect squares with equal row, column and diagonal sums.

events.what_happened: Lucas proved that no 3×3 bimagic square exists (a 3×3 magic square that remains magic when every entry is squared). This is a neighbouring question, not the one asked. Cited as a fact in the introduction of Auel–Singer (2026, reference [42]); Lucas's original was not opened and the venue is not checked.
events.delivers: Impossibility of a 3×3 bimagic square, i.e. a magic square whose entries are squares AND which stays magic after squaring. The bimagic condition is stronger than and different from the condition asked here, so this does not decide whether a 3×3 magic square of nine distinct squares exists.
events.remains: The whole problem as stated.
events.direction: Negative, but for the neighbouring bimagic question. It does not cut against the distinct-squares question either way.

events.what_happened: Yuriy Chebrakov, in an email dated 2 Feb 2000 (forwarded to and quoted on the Problems & Puzzles page, primepuzzles.net puzz_079), says: 'I have very simple proofs that Magic Squares 3x3 from Fibonacci and square numbers do not exist.' He describes a planned paper, 'Non-existing Magic Squares', with a target of March 2000. I found no such paper and no argument for the claim on the page.
events.delivers: A claimed, unexhibited nonexistence proof for 3×3 magic squares from square numbers. The quoted scope ('Fibonacci and square numbers') does not state distinct entries. No argument is reproduced.
events.remains: Everything, since no argument is shown.
events.doubts: No argument shown and no publication found. The date is the email's; when the email first appeared in public writing is not dated on the page. The page itself calls Chebrakov 'a Russian Professor who is prone to publish a paper (or a book) with a proof about the non existence', and says the puzzle has 'no one example of this kind of magic squares' known.
events.direction: Claims the answer is no, without an exhibited argument.

events.what_happened: Lee Sallows, 'The Lost Theorem', The Mathematical Intelligencer (1997), per the Wikipedia reference list; the article itself was not opened. A near miss: all rows, all columns and one diagonal of his 3×3 square sum to the same square number, and the other diagonal fails.
events.delivers: A near miss: a 3×3 square of squares with equal sums on all lines except one diagonal. It does not satisfy the question's conditions and is not a solution.
events.remains: The whole problem as stated.
events.directly_checkable: The near-miss square can be checked by hand; I did not reproduce its entries because the article was not opened.
events.direction: Neither: a near miss that fails the magic condition on one diagonal.
events.object: A 3×3 array with all rows, all columns and one diagonal summing to one square number; the other diagonal fails. Entries not read by me.

events.what_happened: Christian Boyer's 2005 prize offer of €1,000 plus a bottle of champagne for a complete 3×3 magic square of squares with seven, eight or nine distinct squared integers, plus a prize for showing impossibility; and his survey 'Some notes on the magic squares of squares problem', The Mathematical Intelligencer 27(2) (2005), pp. 52–64, which Auel–Singer cite as 2005 (Wikipedia gives 2008 for the same volume and pages). Prizes are not results. The survey was not opened.
events.delivers: No resolution; a prize offer and a survey. Nothing in the record beyond the citation, since the survey was not read.
events.remains: The whole problem as stated.
events.doubts: Engagement with the survey was not assessed because I did not open it.
events.direction: None.

events.what_happened: On primepuzzles puzz_079: Jean-Claude Rosa (added around 2004) gives a proof that a 3×3 magic square of squared primes cannot exist, saying he had not obtained Chebrakov's full proof. Christian Boyer (note dated 30/10/04) corrects one step of Rosa's argument and gives an alternative argument that a 3×3 magic square of squares of primes cannot exist. Neither argument is reproduced on the page.
events.revisions: Boyer's correction is dated 30/10/04 on the page; Rosa's addition is only given as 'about four years after' 2000.
events.delivers: Restricted to squares of primes (every entry a squared prime). That is a subclass of the problem, not the general case.
events.remains: Every 3×3 magic square of distinct squares whose entries are not all squared primes, i.e. almost all of the problem.
events.doubts: Arguments not reproduced; the page itself records that Rosa did not have Chebrakov's full proof, and that Boyer corrected a step of Rosa's.
events.direction: Negative, restricted to squared primes.

events.what_happened: Landon W. Rabern, in the Rose-Hulman Undergraduate Mathematics Journal, vol. 4 issue 1 (2003): conditional results on 3×3 magic squares of squares under the assumption that all entries are coprime, and a conjecture. Per the primepuzzles summary; the paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Conditional restrictions on where primes may sit under a coprimality hypothesis. Not an unconditional result.
events.remains: The unconditional problem, and every case where the coprimality assumption fails.

checked_by.who: Rose-Hulman Undergraduate Mathematics Journal (student journal; editorial process not inspected)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record that accepted the paper for publication
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (refereeing details not inspected)

events.doubts: Conditional result only; the journal's refereeing was not inspected.
events.direction: Neither; partial and conditional.

events.what_happened: Jailton C. Ferreira, 'On the 3×3 magic square constructed with nine distinct square numbers', arXiv:1506.06621 (math.GM), 4 pages. The abstract states: 'A proof that there is no 3×3 magic square constructed with nine distinct square numbers is given.' The argument, as read in the ar5iv extraction: the grid entries lie in N with common sum x; the centre is x/3; the remaining entries are written as the centre plus or minus two differences Δ1 and Δ2 (distinctness needs Δ1 ≠ 0, Δ2 ≠ 0, Δ1 ≠ Δ2); a parametrisation of consecutive square differences gives n² + m² = 2e², and the case w = 0 forces Δ1 = Δ2. The paper concludes: 'There is no magic square constructed with nine distinct square numbers.' The arXiv PDF text could not be decoded; the ar5iv HTML was read.
events.revisions: v1 submitted 24 Apr 2015; v2 revised 26 Jun 2015 (the version the abstract page shows). No journal reference.
events.delivers: Claims a full nonexistence proof for 3×3 magic squares with nine distinct square numbers in N. The paper does not say whether 0 belongs to N, so whether 0 is an allowed entry is not settled by the text.
events.remains: Nothing, if the argument is correct. If it is not, the whole problem.
events.directly_checkable: The argument is elementary algebra on a 3×3 linear system plus a single Diophantine parametrisation, checkable by hand from the four-page paper. I did not complete that check; I read the steps through the ar5iv extraction only.
events.doubts: (1) No refereed publication, no review, and no published comment found. (2) I read the key steps only through an extraction, not line by line; the parametrisation of consecutive square differences and the case analysis that discards w = −2n are where a gap would be looked for. (3) The domain is N with no statement about 0. (4) Hill (2025) states the same theorem and does not cite Ferreira; Auel–Singer (2026) does not cite Ferreira either; the Wikipedia article (edited 23 Sep 2026 per the page) does not mention it. The silence of later work is a finding, not a verdict on the argument.
events.direction: Claims the answer is no: no such 3×3 square exists.

events.what_happened: Christian Woll, 'A Partial Residue Categorization of the Magic Square of Squares', arXiv:1809.03067. v1 10 Sep 2018; v2 14 Sep 2018, marked withdrawn in the submission history; v3 9 Nov 2018 (the current version). The abstract opens: 'It is unknown at present whether a magic square of squared integers exists.' The paper categorises the residues of such a square for primes dividing the centre, gives a solution over a finite field, and states conjectures about which residues occur.
events.revisions: v1 10 Sep 2018 (7 KB); v2 14 Sep 2018 (withdrawn); v3 9 Nov 2018 (6 KB, current, comments '9 pages, no figures').
events.delivers: Restrictions on residues of a magic square of squares for primes dividing the centre, plus a finite-field solution and conjectures. Restricted to residue structure and finite fields; it does not decide existence over the integers.
events.remains: Existence (and nonexistence) over the integers with nine distinct entries.
events.doubts: v2 was withdrawn; the reasons quoted in a search extraction ('missed p=13, typos, stronger restrictions') are not confirmed from the current listing, which carries no withdrawal note in its comments field.

withdrawn.what: v2 (14 Sep 2018) is marked withdrawn in the arXiv submission history; the reasons quoted in a search extraction were 'missed p=13, typos, stronger restrictions than the corollaries have already been given in the literature'. Not verified from the page itself.

events.direction: Neither; structural restrictions, a finite-field solution and conjectures. No object exhibited over the integers.

events.what_happened: Onno Cain, 'Gaussian Integers, Rings, Finite Fields, and the Magic Square of Squares', arXiv:1908.03236 (math.RA, math.NT), 15 pages; v1 8 Aug 2019, v2 12 Aug 2019. It shows the 3×3 magic square of squares problem is equivalent to solving quartic polynomials with factorisation constraints over an abelian extension of Q, analyses the Gaussian-integer case to give a search method, and states conjectures about finite fields and Z/nZ.
events.delivers: An equivalence to quartic polynomials and a search method for the Gaussian-integer case. Conjectures only for finite fields and Z/nZ. No claim about existence or nonexistence over the integers.
events.remains: The integer question as stated.
events.direction: Neither; a reduction and a search method.

events.what_happened: 'A New Transformation of the Magic Square of Squares', arXiv:2310.12164 (math.HO, cross-listed math.NT), one version, submitted 1 Oct 2023. The author is printed as 'Christian Wolird' on the arXiv abstract page; I did not confirm the spelling against any other source. The abstract shows a 3-to-1 correspondence between arithmetic triplets of Gaussian squares and Pythagorean triples, and a conditional 'backwards' result: a solution to the puzzle would generate non-trivial near-miss solutions in the Gaussian integers.
events.revisions: v1 only (1 Oct 2023, 1,033 KB, 11 pages, 15 figures).
events.delivers: A correspondence and a conditional statement over the Gaussian integers. The abstract does not claim to resolve the 3×3 case over the integers.
events.remains: The integer question as stated.
events.direction: Neither; conditional and over a different ring.

events.what_happened: Tony Várilly-Alvarado (Rice) gave a talk, 'Perfect Cuboids and Magic Squares of Squares', at the Penn Mathematics Colloquium on 30 Nov 2022 and at an Emory algebra colloquium on 4 Dec 2023, using one abstract. He argues heuristically, via the geometry of a 'Parker surface' with finitely many rational and elliptic curves, that a 3×3 magic square of distinct squares is highly unlikely, and states his belief that none exists. A Numberphile video with him, 'Magic Squares of Squares (are PROBABLY impossible)', was posted 13 Jun 2023. The talk and video were not opened; the details come from search extractions.
events.revisions: Same abstract reused at Emory (4 Dec 2023) and in a Numberphile video (13 Jun 2023, per search extraction).
events.delivers: A heuristic argument that the answer is no; not a proof. It states that the 3×3 distinct-squares question is open.
events.remains: The whole problem as stated.
events.doubts: Heuristic only, by the speaker's own description. A search extraction also reports that Várilly-Alvarado's 'doubt' is a belief rather than a proof.
events.direction: Leans negative (heuristic belief that no square exists). Not a proof either way.

events.what_happened: On the primepuzzles puzz_079 page, Arkadiusz Wesolowski gives constructions of 3×3 magic squares with 5 and 6 perfect-square entries (comments dated 29 Dec 2018, 19 Dec 2019 and 20 Jan 2020), and challenges readers to find a family with 7 perfect squares.
events.revisions: Further comments 19 Dec 2019 and 20 Jan 2020 on the same page.
events.delivers: Near misses with five and six perfect-square entries. Not all nine entries are squares, so this does not solve the question; it is a partial construction.
events.remains: Every 3×3 square with nine perfect-square entries, distinct.
events.directly_checkable: The constructions are small explicit arrays and could be checked by hand; the arrays were not reproduced in this record.
events.direction: Neither; partial near misses.
events.object: 3×3 magic squares with five and six perfect-square entries (a partial near miss, not a solution). Explicit entries were not read into this record.

events.what_happened: Andrew Bremner, 'On squares of squares', Acta Arithmetica 88 (1999), 289–297, gives a 3×3 magic square with seven of nine entries perfect squares, the closest known example. Wikipedia dates Bremner's attempt to 1999; a search extraction gives 1997 as the discovery year. The paper itself was not opened; OEIS A221669 (search extraction) says this is the only known 3×3 magic square with seven squares and that none is known with eight or nine. Bremner's sequel 'On squares of squares II', Acta Arithmetica 99 (2001), 289–308, is listed in Auel–Singer's references and was not opened.
events.revisions: Sequel: Acta Arithmetica 99 (2001), not opened. Discovery year 1997 per a search extraction; first public writing not pinned down.
events.delivers: A near miss with seven of nine entries squares. Not all nine entries are squares and not a solution.
events.remains: Every 3×3 square with nine perfect-square entries, distinct.
events.directly_checkable: The seven-square example can be checked by hand; not reproduced here.
events.direction: Neither; near miss.
events.object: A 3×3 magic square with seven of its nine entries perfect squares, the other two not squares. Entries not read by me.

events.what_happened: Scott Kominers, 'Center-Zero Magic Squares of Squares over Number Fields', a PDF on the author's website (search extraction only; not opened). It studies proper 3×3 magic squares of distinct squares in a number field with centre 0. It states that no quadratic number field admits such a square, and that degree 4 suffices via congruent numbers (rational right triangles of area n give infinitely many over Q(i, √n)). The author and date were taken from the search result; no arXiv identifier or date was found.
events.delivers: Restricted to squares over number fields with centre zero. It does not decide the integer question; the centre-zero condition is a restriction the question does not impose.
events.remains: The integer question as stated, and the non-centre-zero cases.
events.doubts: Undated; not opened; the result is taken from a search extraction.
events.direction: Neither; a restricted-case result.

events.what_happened: Giancarlo Labruna, master's thesis 'Magic Squares of Squares of Order Three Over Finite Fields', Montclair State University, 2018, as described in the 2021 Hengeveld–Labruna–Li abstract (search extraction). The thesis was not opened. Per the description it shows that a magic square of squares over a finite field of characteristic greater than 3 can have only 3, 5, 7 or 9 distinct entries, and classifies those over characteristic 2.
events.delivers: Finite-field results only; the description says nothing about the integers.
events.remains: The integer question as stated.
events.doubts: Not opened; the description reports the thesis's claims as 'we claim', while the 2021 paper says 'we show' about related results.
events.direction: Neither; finite-field analogue.

events.what_happened: Stewart Hengeveld, Giancarlo Labruna and Aihua Li, 'magic squares of squares over finite fields', in Commutative Algebra: 150 Years with Roger and Sylvia Wiegand (AMS Contemporary Mathematics), 2021 (per search extraction; not opened). For any odd prime p a magic square over Z/pZ has an odd number of distinct entries; there are infinitely many primes p for which magic squares of squares with nine distinct elements exist over Z/pZ, which the authors say answers, for finite fields, LaBar's 1984 question about the integers; for p ≡ 1 (mod 120) there are examples with 3, 5, 7 or 9 distinct entries.
events.delivers: Existence for infinitely many primes p over Z/pZ. This is a finite-field analogue, not a result over the integers; it establishes nothing about the integer question.
events.remains: The integer question as stated.
events.directly_checkable: Finite-field constructions could be checked by computer or by hand for a given p; not done.
events.direction: Positive over finite fields; no bearing on integer existence.

events.what_happened: MathPages article 'Magic Square of Squares' (kmath417; author not named; undated on the page, with a link to an 'updated version'). It states the open question at the start, shows that every line through the centre is an arithmetic progression, and gives Proposition 1: a square whose centre has at most four two-square representations fails the outer-line conditions. The article says this 'doesn't completely rule out the existence of a magic square of squares'.
events.revisions: Page points to an 'updated version' at kmath417/kmath417.htm; not opened.
events.delivers: A restricted partial result for centres with at most four two-square representations. Not a resolution.
events.remains: Centres with more representations, and the whole problem.
events.directly_checkable: The parametric identities can be checked by hand.
events.doubts: Undated page; the restricted proposition is stated by the author as not completing the proof.
events.direction: Neither; restricted partial result that leans toward the answer 'no' in the restricted case.

events.what_happened: A document titled 'The Proof for Non-existence of Magic Square of Squares in Order Three' on academia.edu (search listing, id 89159599), which claims a proof that no magic square of squares of order three exists. The page returned HTTP 403 to my fetch, so the document was not read. Author, date and argument are unknown.
events.delivers: Claimed nonexistence for order three, unverified.
events.remains: Unknown; not read.
events.doubts: Not readable by me, so I cannot assess the argument, its scope, or whether it duplicates Ferreira's or Hill's.
events.direction: Claims the answer is no. Unverified.

events.what_happened: Nick Rome and Shuntaro Yamagishi, 'On the existence of magic squares of powers', arXiv:2406.09364, first posted 13 Jun 2024. For each d ≥ 2 there is n0(d) such that n×n magic squares of dth powers exist for all n ≥ n0(d); for squares, n×n magic squares of squares exist for every n ≥ 4, settling a Várilly-Alvarado conjecture. Method: Hardy–Littlewood circle method. Published in Research in Number Theory 11(4), article 91, 23 Sep 2025 (DOI 10.1007/s40993-025-00671-5, per the ISTA repository record).
events.revisions: v1 13 Jun 2024 (30 KB); v2 4 Sep 2024 (18 KB, current on arXiv). The v2 comment reads: 'Updated version features revised algorithm making computer search unnecessary as well as proper credit for the work of Flores.' Journal version 23 Sep 2025.
events.delivers: Existence of n×n magic squares of squares for every n ≥ 4, and of nth-power squares for large n. Does not cover n = 3. The paper's own note on the 3×3 case, as quoted in a search extraction, is that it 'seems plausible that perhaps there are no 3×3 magic squares of squares, or that they are remarkably rare'. Whether the squares must have distinct entries was not confirmed: the arXiv abstract page and the PDF text I could read did not state it.
events.remains: The 3×3 case in full, with or without distinct entries. Whether the n ≥ 4 squares are distinct is not established by my reading.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record that accepted and published the paper
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper on 23 Sep 2025 (refereeing process not inspected)

events.doubts: None specific. The arXiv PDF text could not be decoded, so I did not read the proof; the claims above come from the abstract, the abstract page, and the ISTA record.
events.direction: Cuts toward existence for n ≥ 4; silent on n = 3.
events.object: Non-constructive existence for each n ≥ 4 via the circle method, as the abstract describes. The v2 comment says a revised algorithm replaced an earlier computer search, which is computation, not AI. No explicit 3×3 object.

events.what_happened: Daniel Flores, 'A circle method approach to K-multimagic squares', arXiv:2406.08161 (math.NT, cross-listed math.CO), first posted 12 Jun 2024; v2 1 Jan 2025 (fixed a mistake in the proof of Lemma 4.1). It bounds the smallest order N2(K) of a nontrivial K-multimagic square (a square that stays magic after raising entries to the kth power for 2 ≤ k ≤ K) by 2K(K+1)+1, and deduces infinitely many prime-valued examples. Rome and Yamagishi's v2 comment credits this work.
events.delivers: A general order bound for multimagic squares. It is about powers beyond squaring (and K = 2 is the bimagic condition), not about magic squares of distinct squares. It says nothing about order 3.
events.remains: The whole problem as stated.
events.direction: Neither for this problem; a neighbouring multimagic result.

events.what_happened: Oscar Hill (sole author), arXiv:2510.08286 [math.GM]. v1 (9 Oct 2025) was titled 'An Algebraic Proof of the Nonexistence of 3×3 Magic Squares of Square Integers'. v2 (19 Oct 2025) and v3 (7 Apr 2026, current, header 'arXiv:2510.08286v3 [math.GM] 07 Apr 2026') are titled 'On Arithmetic Progressions and a Proof of the Nonexistence of Magic Squares of Squares'. The abstract: the paper studies consecutive, equally summed arithmetic progressions of odd numbers, their offsets and sums, 'before using them to prove that no 3×3 magic squares of distinct square integers exist'. Theorem 3.1 reads 'It is impossible to construct a 3×3 magic square consisting solely of square integers.' The argument: Section 3.1 sets the linear relations of a 3×3 magic square, forces three AP pairs with common sum D1 and two APs with sum D2 (assumed positive 'by symmetry'), defines ratios β1, β2; Lemma 3.2 asserts Σp_A = Σp_B in three cases; an identity (eq. 29, expanded in eq. 30) with odd-power coefficients forces β1 = 1, hence 𝒫1² = 𝒫2², and the paper concludes 𝒫1 = 𝒫2 = 𝒫3, 'contradicting our initial premise'.
events.revisions: v1 9 Oct 2025 (title 'An Algebraic Proof of the Nonexistence of 3×3 Magic Squares of Square Integers'); v2 19 Oct 2025 (retitled; comment 'Updated notation, particularly around singular APs, to be clearer to understand' on the current listing); v3 7 Apr 2026 (current). No changelog on the page.
events.delivers: Claims a full nonexistence proof for 3×3 magic squares of distinct integers that are squares, in the sense of the problem as stated. Scope: integer entries only. Rational, Gaussian and finite-field variants are not addressed. Zero entries: Section 3.1 takes the entries in ℕ0 (zero included), while the introduction defines magic squares of positive integers, and nothing explicitly excludes a zero magic constant or a zero entry.
events.remains: Nothing, if the argument holds. If it fails, the whole problem. The paper says nothing about rational or Gaussian-integer variants.
events.directly_checkable: The argument is elementary algebra on explicit equations (the 3×3 linear system, the AP offsets, Lemma 3.2 and the identity in eqs. 29 to 30), checkable by hand from arXiv 2510.08286v3. I did not complete that check; I read the structure through the HTML extraction, which did not show every derivation.
events.doubts: (1) No refereed publication, no journal reference on the arXiv page, no review, comment, or Lean formalisation found in searches. (2) Zero entries: Section 3.1 uses ℕ0 and assumes D1, D2 > 0 'by symmetry'; the introduction says positive integers; no sentence excludes a zero magic constant. (3) The extraction did not show the derivation of 𝒫1² = 𝒫2² from equation (3), nor the full case analysis of Lemma 3.2, so those steps are where a gap would be looked for; I could not verify them. (4) The paper does not cite Ferreira (2015), which states the same theorem, nor Bremner, Boyer, or Auel–Singer; its only cited prior work is Rome–Yamagishi, and it says Rome and Yamagishi 'did not disprove the existence' of a 3×3 square. (5) The later Auel–Singer paper (8 Sep 2026) calls the distinct-integer question open since the 18th century and does not cite Hill; Wikipedia (edited 23 Sep 2026 per the page, read by WebFetch) lists the problem as unsolved and does not mention Hill. (6) The title changed between v1 and v2, dropping '3×3' from the title while the abstract keeps it.
events.direction: Claims the answer is no: no 3×3 magic square of distinct square integers exists. Cuts against the open status stated by Wikipedia and Auel–Singer, not against any exhibited object.

events.what_happened: Asher Auel and Benjamin Singer, 'The algebraic geometry of 3-by-3 magic squares of squares', arXiv:2609.09351 (math.AG, math.NT), submitted 8 Sep 2026 (43 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables; one version). They study the surface V parametrising 3×3 magic squares of squares, a singular complete intersection of six quadrics in P^8: geometric automorphisms via Gale duality, topological invariants and Hodge diamond of a resolution, an explicit rank-518 sublattice of the geometric Picard group (Hodge bound 544), and del Pezzo, K3 and Enriques surfaces as coordinate projections. Appendix A (Proposition A.1) shows the Fano scheme of lines on V is empty, and Remark A.2 says no lines meet the distinct locus. The introduction says the authors' work 'provides the first steps toward realizing this approach' (an étale Brauer–Manin obstruction) without computing it.
events.revisions: v1 only (8 Sep 2026, 48 KB as listed).
events.delivers: Geometry of the parametrising surface and a partial lattice computation. States that the question 'has been open since the 18th century' (abstract) and that it is 'still unknown whether a 3×3 magic square of squares exists over the rational numbers' (introduction). The Fano-scheme result is a sub-result about lines on the surface; it does not decide the existence question for distinct integer squares.
events.remains: Existence (and nonexistence) for distinct integer squares, and over the rationals.
events.directly_checkable: The Picard-rank computations use Magma scripts, described in the paper as modified versions of Stoll's code. Magma is computer algebra, not AI. No Lean build.
events.doubts: Recent and unrefereed. The paper does not discuss Hill's 2025 claim or Ferreira's 2015 claim, so it is silent on whether the open-status statement knows of them.
events.direction: Does not settle existence either way. States the distinct-integer question is open.
events.object: None exhibited as a 3×3 magic square of distinct squares. The paper treats the surface V whose rational points correspond to such squares, and it presents new families over biquadratic fields, which are not integer examples with distinct entries.

disputes.summary: Two claimed proofs that no 3×3 magic square of nine distinct squares exists: Ferreira (arXiv 1506.06621, first posted 24 Apr 2015) and Hill (arXiv 2510.08286, first posted 9 Oct 2025). Hill's paper does not cite Ferreira's. Neither has a found referee report, journal acceptance, or published comment, and no source assesses either against the other. Whether either counts is not decided here. A third, undated academia.edu document makes the same claim and was not readable.

Year of Boyer's Mathematical Intelligencer article 'Some notes on the magic squares of squares problem' (vol. 27, pp. 52–64): 2005 per Auel–Singer's reference list [9]; the Wikipedia reference list (as read through WebFetch) gives 2008 for the same volume and pages.

summary: Searches (47 web searches, about 25 primary sources opened, including arXiv abstracts and extractions of full text where the PDF did not decode) find no settlement of the 3×3 distinct-squares question that has been accepted by referees or the literature as of 11 Oct 2026. The one event that matches the question as stated is Oscar Hill's arXiv 2510.08286 (sole author; v1 9 Oct 2025, retitled in v2 19 Oct 2025, v3 7 Apr 2026), which claims Theorem 3.1: no 3×3 magic square of distinct square integers exists, by consecutive equal-sum AP pairs, Lemma 3.2, and an identity forcing 𝒫1² = 𝒫2². I read its structure through the HTML extraction, not line by line. Close reading raises three points I could not resolve: Section 3 works in ℕ0, so zero entries are allowed though the introduction says positive integers; the sign of D1 and D2 is assumed 'by symmetry'; and the derivation of 𝒫1² = 𝒫2² and the case analysis of Lemma 3.2 are asserted without visible steps. Against the claim: no journal, referee, comment or formal check was found; the Auel–Singer paper (8 Sep 2026) calls the distinct-integer question open since the 18th century and does not cite Hill; and Wikipedia (edited 23 Sep 2026 per the page) lists it as unsolved without mentioning Hill. The earlier claimed proof by Ferreira (4 pages, 2015) has the same status: the ar5iv extraction shows the same architecture (centre x/3, differences Δ1 and Δ2, a parametrised contradiction at w = 0), with the domain N and no statement about 0, and no one has engaged with it in the sources I found. Within the window, two results are real mathematics but do not touch n = 3: Rome and Yamagishi (13 Jun 2024; journal 23 Sep 2025) prove existence of n×n magic squares of squares for every n ≥ 4 and say the 3×3 case may have none or they are rare; Flores (12 Jun 2024) bounds the order of K-multimagic squares, not this problem. Auel–Singer (2026) is an algebraic-geometry study of the parametrising surface with a Fano-lines sub-result; it leaves existence open. Before 2024 the record holds near misses (Sallows 1997; Bremner 1999 with seven of nine squares, the closest known), restricted or conditional partial results (Rabern 2003; Woll 2018, v2 withdrawn; Cain 2019; Wolird 2023 over the Gaussian integers; Boyer and Rosa 2004 for squared primes; Kominers, undated, centre-zero over number fields), finite-field results (Labruna 2018 thesis; Hengeveld–Labruna–Li 2021), an unpublished 2000 claim by Chebrakov, and Várilly-Alvarado's 2022 heuristic that the answer is no. The Penn talk is dated 30 Nov 2022 from the search extraction; the Emory and Numberphile pages were not opened. AI: no AI system is credited with anything in this problem. The one AI disclosure is in Auel–Singer's 'Statement on AI Usage' (arXiv 2609.09351 html): 'The second author used Claude Opus 5, courtesy of Dartmouth College, in the editing process to check for typos, notational inconsistencies, and errors, as well as to clean up code to make it more presentable.' followed by 'All mathematics and writing within this paper are entirely the work of the authors.' That is proofreading and code cleanup, not load-bearing, so ai.systems is empty for that event and none_found is false. Hill's, Ferreira's and Rome–Yamagishi's full texts name no system. Several AI-specific searches (LLM, ChatGPT, Gemini, AlphaEvolve, Aristotle, Erdős-problem trackers, Gaussian near-miss) found no AI claim on this problem; the unrelated AI results I saw (an AI-assisted magic-hexagon result reported second-hand for August 2026, and Erdős-problem work) are not about 3×3 squares of squares. Two source errors I noticed: a search summary attributed the n ≥ 4 result to Bremner and coauthors, but Rome and Yamagishi are the authors; and Boyer's survey year differs between sources (see disputes). Gardner's 1996 US$100 prize and Boyer's 2005 offer were both reported unclaimed in 2025 sources; I did not confirm the current status on Boyer's site, which I could not reach.
competing_reading: Read Hill (and, earlier, Ferreira) as settling the problem as stated: an elementary, explicit nonexistence proof of a 3×3 square of nine distinct integer squares, posted with a full theorem statement; the 2026 Auel–Singer and Wikipedia statements may simply reflect that the preprint has not yet reached specialists, and the zero-entry and unshown-step points may be presentational. On that reading the question has been answered since October 2025, and the record should treat Hill as the resolving event, with the AI disclosure in Auel–Singer irrelevant to it. Against that reading: neither claim has been refereed, nobody with a record in this area has engaged with either, a 2026 team that writes about this exact surface calls the question open, and the Hill argument leaves two places (the ℕ0 domain with the unforced sign assumption, and the unshown step to 𝒫1² = 𝒫2²) that a referee would test first. Those points can be checked by hand and I did not finish checking them.
what_would_settle_it: A referee report or journal acceptance of Hill's argument (or of Ferreira's); a line-by-line check of Lemma 3.2 and the step from eq. (3) to 𝒫1² = 𝒫2², plus its treatment of zero entries and of a zero magic constant; a formal Lean or Coq check of either argument; an erratum, a withdrawal, or a rebuttal from Hill, Ferreira or the Auel–Singer authors; an update to Wikipedia's article citing either preprint; or an actual 3×3 square of nine distinct squares (none is known, and Wikipedia reports brute-force searches unsuccessful up to 10^14).
